items.title: SAP QA Testing Services for BTP-Based Custom Apps: A Different Approach than Classic ABAP?
items.author: toddbravosap
items.text:
SAP’s August 2025 update to the ABAP Extensibility Guide aligned its technical recommendations with the clean core level model, adding guidance for ABAP Cloud development and governance for classic ABAP code. That guidance helps teams choose between building an extension on the S/4HANA stack and building it side by side on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP). It also shapes how I plan SAP QA testing services, because each choice creates different test boundaries. 
 A classic Z-report and its BAdI live in one system, with one database and one transport path. A BTP app calls S/4HANA through APIs, publishes events, and ships through a pipeline. In this article, I follow one custom app through every test layer, compare it with its classic ABAP equivalent, and close with the six-step plan I recommend to teams starting this work.

items.title: Purchase Order Accruals - Customizing basics
items.author: Ujhelyi_Zsuzsi
items.text:
To set up the Accrual Engine with the necessary Customizing settings in SAP, you'll need to follow these steps. You can access these settings through the IMG (Implementation Guide) using transaction code SPRO or directly via ACEIMG for Accruals Management. Here’s a step-by-step guide: 
 Accessing Customizing 
 Transaction codes : Use SPRO for the general IMG or ACEIMG specifically for Accruals Management. 
 Customizing Purchase Order Items for Accrual 
 Path in SPRO : 
 Financial Accounting (New) → General Ledger Accounting (New) → Periodic Processing → Accruals Management → Define Which Purchase Order Items Are To Be Accrued 
 Configuration : Define the criteria for which purchase orders or items should be accrued. This could be based on various attributes like procurement type, purchase order type, material group, etc. 
 Define Accrual Algorithms 
 Path in SPRO : 
 Financial Accounting (New) → General Ledger Accounting (New) → Periodic Processing → Accruals Management → Define Accrual Algorithms 
 Configuration : Set up the algorithms that will calculate the accrual amounts. This could be based on different criteria such as linear, weighted, or custom algorithms. 
 Define Review and Approval Procedures (not mandatory) 
 Path in SPRO : 
 Financial Accounting (New) → General Ledger Accounting (New) → Periodic Processing → Accruals Management → Define Review/Approval Procedures for Accruals 
 Configuration : Specify whether a manual review and/or approval process is required for accrual amounts at the end of each period. Define the workflow and approval levels as necessary. 
 Assign Accrual Accounts 
 Path in SPRO : 
 Financial Accounting (New) → General Ledger Accounting (New) → Periodic Processing → Accruals Management → Define Accrual Accounts 
 Configuration : Map the relevant G/L accounts to be used for accrual postings. These accounts will record the accrued expenses and liabilities in the general ledger. 
 Additional Settings (if required) 
 Depending on your organization's requirements, you may need to configure additional settings such as tolerance limits, reporting settings, and integration with other modules (e.g., Materials Management, Controlling). 

 Customizing Settings for the Accrual Engine 
 The Accrual Engine is a generic tool, so you'll need to focus on the settings that are relevant for purchase order accruals. 
 Steps: 
 Access the IMG for Accruals Management : 
 Transaction code: ACEIMG 
 Define the General Settings : 
 Path : Accruals Management → General Settings → Define General Settings 
 Configuration : Configure the basic settings such as tolerance limits, rounding rules, and other general parameters. 
 Define Accrual Algorithms : 
 Path : Accruals Management → General Settings → Define Accrual Algorithms 
 Configuration : Set up the algorithms to be used for calculating accruals. This could include linear, weighted, or custom algorithms specific to your business needs. 
 Define Accrual Accounts : 
 Path : Accruals Management → General Settings → Define Accrual Accounts 
 Configuration : Map the relevant G/L accounts that will be used for posting the accrual entries. 
 Define Accrual Types : 
 Path : Accruals Management → General Settings → Define Accrual Types 
 Configuration : Set up the different accrual types relevant for purchase orders, such as goods receipt, invoice receipt, etc. 
 Customizing Settings Specific for Purchase Order Accruals 
 These settings are tailored specifically for the application of purchase order accruals. 
 Steps: 
 Define Which Purchase Order Items Are to Be Accrued : 
 Path : Accruals Management → Purchase Order Accruals → Define Which Purchase Order Items Are To Be Accrued 
 Configuration : Specify the criteria for determining which purchase order items should be included in the accrual process. This can be based on attributes like purchase order type, procurement type, material group, etc. 
 Define Accrual Methods for Purchase Order Items : 
 Path : Accruals Management → Purchase Order Accruals → Define Accrual Methods for Purchase Order Items 
 Configuration : Assign the specific accrual algorithms to the purchase order items. This defines how the accruals will be calculated. 
 Define Review/Approval Procedures for Purchase Order Accruals : 
 Path : Accruals Management → Purchase Order Accruals → Define Review/Approval Procedures for Accruals 
 Configuration : Specify whether a manual review and/or approval process is required for the accrued amounts at the end of each period. Define the necessary workflow and approval levels. 
 Additional Settings : 
 Path : Accruals Management → Purchase Order Accruals → Additional Settings 
 Configuration : Depending on your organization's requirements, you might need to configure additional settings such as tolerance limits specific to purchase orders, reporting settings, and integration settings with other modules like Materials Management or Controlling. 

 Customizing Basic Settings 
 In the transaction "Accruals Management - IMG" (ACEIMG), under Basic Settings, the following activities are relevant for purchase order accruals: 
 Assign Company Codes : Assign the company codes to the Accrual Engine for which purchase order accruals will be posted. 
 Define Accrual Item Types : This is one of the main activities in the Accrual Engine. Accrual item types are a central concept in the Accrual Engine. To understand this entity, it is beneficial to first grasp the underlying concept of accrual objects. 
 These settings ensure that the Accrual Engine is configured to handle purchase order accruals according to your company's requirements.

items.title: Purchase Order Accruals- High level purpose and basic examples
items.author: Ujhelyi_Zsuzsi
items.text:
Business context and overview 
 As soon as there are liabilities to a third party, for example to a supplier, 
 but the related costs have not yet been posted, accruals need to be 
 posted. 
 By posting accruals in the system, the relevant costs are allocated to 
 the fiscal period in which they occurred. 
 The posting of accruals is typically a period-end closing activity 
 because it is often not known until period end to what extent accruals 
 are required. 
 Optional Extension: Accruals for Purchasing to Stock or Fixed Asset 
 Default behavior: Accruals are only generated for purchase orders that involve cost assignments (such as cost centers or internal orders), not for those that go into material stock or fixed assets. 
 Exception:  It is possible to enable accruals for purchase orders that post to material stock or fixed assets. This requires implementing specific Business Add-Ins (BAdIs). 
 Guidance:  For technical details and sample source code for the BAdI implementations, refer to consulting note 2888110 - "Enable accruals for purchase orders to stock". 

 Overview: Features 
 With the new Purchase Order Accruals application: 
 Automatically calculate and post purchase order accruals. 
 Built on the new SAP S/4HANA Accrual Engine, offering flexible customization for accrual calculation and posting. 
 Key features: 
 ** optional review/approval process:** Activate through Customizing to review and approve monthly accrual amounts. 
 Monitoring and review screens:  Available for SAP GUI in release 1809, with Fiori apps planned for release 1909. 
 Cloud availability:  Purchase order accruals available in SAP S/4HANA Cloud 1811. 
 Basic Principle 
 At the end of each fiscal period, the Purchase Order Accruals application performs the following: 
 Calculates accrual amounts for purchase order items by evaluating planned data, such as: 
 Delivery schedules with planned delivery dates, determining cumulated planned costs up to the period's end. 
 Other data like non-valuated goods receipts. 
 Assumes that cumulated planned costs reflect actual costs at the period's end. 
 If cumulated actual costs are less than planned, the system proposes the difference as the accrual amount. 
 Activates a review process by default, as the proposed accrual amount is assumption-based. This review process can be configured to examine: 
 Proposed accrual amounts. 
 Planned costs. 
 Fine-Grained Posting of Accruals: Audit-Save 

 The Purchase Order Accruals application operates with precision: 
 Calculates, reviews, and posts accruals at the detailed level of individual purchase order items. 
 Aims to determine accrual amounts in a reliable, reproducible, and audit-compliant manner. 
 Alternative approach: 
 Estimate accrual amounts based on historical data. 
 While applicable in some cases, this method generally produces unreliable results. 
 Main Process Steps 
 Purchase Order Accruals Process: 
 Creation of Purchase Order 
 Create purchase orders using transaction ME21N in MM-PUR. 
 Each purchase order is automatically transferred to the Accrual Engine based on Customizing settings. 
 Initial Data Load:  Transfer existing purchase orders using transaction POAC_MM2ACE_TRANSFER. 
 2. Display Accrual Objects 
 View monthly accrual amounts calculated by the system using transaction POACTREE03. 

 3. Optional Review and Approval Process 
 At the end of each fiscal period, a reviewer can adjust proposed accrual amounts or planned costs. 
 Generate proposal amounts using transaction ACEPROPOSALRUN. 
 Review: Perform using transactions FACRARVWBU (for PO owners) or FACRARVWCO (for controllers). Manual adjustments are possible. 
 Approval: Perform using transaction FACRAAPPRVGL. Approval is mandatory for accrual postings if activated. 
 4. Post Accruals 
 Post accrual amounts at the end of each fiscal period using transaction ACEPOSTINGRUN. 
 Purchase Order Accruals: Architecture Big Picture 

 Use-Cases for Accruals: PO Item Without Valuated GR 

 Without Goods Receipts 
 No goods receipts recorded. 
 Accruals proposed based on: 
 Delivery schedule in the purchase order item (past deliveries assumed as received). 
 Straight-line approach (linear distribution of total PO item value). 

 With Non-Valuated Goods Receipts 
 Quantity received is recorded, but no costs posted. 
 Accruals proposed based on recorded quantity multiplied by net price (use accrual method PLN_DSNVGR). 
 Note for Enhanced Limit PO items: Use Expected Value for linearization. 
 3. With Valuated Goods Receipt Postings 
 Goods receipt posts costs as entered quantity multiplied by net price. 
 Accruals proposed based on delivery schedule (past deliveries assumed as received), considering posted costs. 
 4. With Service Entry Sheet Postings 
 Service entry sheet posts costs similarly to valuated goods receipt. 
 Accruals proposed based on straight-line approach (linear distribution between start and end dates). 
 Note: Start and end dates visible for Lean Services approach (Product Type Group 2 “Service”). 
 Relation to Accruals Management 
 The application Purchase Order Accruals is part of the bigger application Accruals Management. 
 Accruals Management bundles all applications that are based on the (new) S/4HANA Accrual Engine. 
 The long-term vision of Accruals Management is to be the single point of entry for managing accruals.

items.title: What's New in Asset Management in SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02
items.author: Fernanda_Rodrigues
items.text:
SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02 marks a turning point for asset management. This release goes well beyond incremental improvements. It delivers a fully operational suite of AI agents that fundamentally changes how maintenance professionals work, moving from isolated transaction execution toward guided, end-to-end workflows where intelligent assistance handles the repetitive, high-volume, and error-prone steps. Alongside the autonomous AI story, FPS02 also introduces meaningful refinements in safety, planning, compliance, and extensibility. 
 SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition (the foundation of SAP Cloud ERP Private) strengthens its position as an integrated, intelligent platform for enterprise asset management in this release. 
 In this post, you will find a curated overview of the most important innovations, grouped by theme and written for maintenance planners, technicians, reliability engineers, and integration professionals who rely on SAP S/4HANA to keep operations running safely and efficiently. 
 For a broader look at what's new across all lines of business in the SAP Cloud ERP Private 2025 FPS02 release, don't miss the SAP Cloud ERP Private FPS02 release overview blog . 
 Table of Contents 
 Autonomous Asset Management: AI Agents in FPS02 
 Maintenance Request Initiation Agent 
 Operational Maintenance Order Planning Agent 
 Maintenance Event Planning Agent 
 Maintenance Job Debrief Agent 
 Equipment Insights Agent 
 Maintenance Task List Agent 
 Further updates on FPS02 release 
 Maintenance notification–based inspection checklist process 
 Inspection checklist further process adjustments 
 SAP Dynamic Forms integration across asset management apps 
 Graphical operation dependencies across maintenance orders 
 Improved visibility for maintenance backlog and event-based planning 
 Collaborative maintenance: maintenance order integration with BNAC 
 Reference Structure: rule framework for change cascading 
 Refurbishment best practice scope items (85R and 85U) 
 Linear Asset Management APIs 
 More information 
 Autonomous Asset Management: AI Agents in FPS02 
 The Asset Operations Assistant: six agents, one coherent workflow 
 The headline story in FPS02 is the Asset Operations Assistant — an AI-powered orchestration layer built on the SAP Joule framework that brings together purpose-built agents covering the full maintenance workflow: from reporting a failure, through order creation, event grouping, and job execution, all the way to technician feedback and knowledge capture. 
 Each agent operates conversationally, in natural language, and always places the human in the loop. No record is created, no status is changed, and no data is submitted without explicit confirmation from the user. This is a deliberate design choice: the agents are meant to accelerate and improve decision quality, not replace the judgment of maintenance professionals. 
 All six agents run on the SAP Joule framework and are accessed through Joule in SAP Cloud ERP Private. 
 *Disclaimer: The Joule Assistants and Agents described in this post are currently available through SAP's Early Adopter Care (EAC) program. General availability is planned to begin in Q4 2026 , with rollout continuing into Q1 2027 . Not all agents require SAP S/4HANA Cloud Private Edition 2025 FPS2 — minimum system requirements vary by agent, and support for additional releases is being continuously extended through downports. For the latest on which releases support which agents, refer to SAP Note 3789370 , which is updated on an ongoing basis, and the SAP Discovery Center . All other innovations covered in this post (embedded AI features, Joule skills, and machine learning scenarios) are generally available with the 2025 FPS2 release unless noted otherwise. This blog is a living document and will be updated as new assistants and agents become available in the coming weeks and months. The information here reflects publicly available SAP product documentation and roadmap materials as of October 2026. All forward-looking statements are subject to change. 

 Maintenance Request Initiation Agent 
 Create maintenance notifications with the details that actually matter in seconds. 
 The Maintenance Request Initiation Agent simplifies one of the most time-consuming daily tasks in asset operations: creating a maintenance notification with all relevant data. A technician in the field can describe an issue in natural language, i.e. a pump seal leaking and the agent takes it from there. 
 The agent identifies the technical object from a partial description, presents a list of matching equipment so the user selects the correct one, and then enriches the notification with failure codes, damage categories, cause codes, and a matching score where catalog master data supports it. It also checks for duplicate notifications on the same equipment before creating a new one — letting the user cancel or create anyway — which keeps the maintenance backlog cleaner and reduces noise and tracking effort. 
 For emergency scenarios , the agent creates both the notification and a maintenance order simultaneously, setting the order directly into execution. Notification type, priority, and start/end dates are captured in a single conversational exchange, with a confirmation step before any record is written to the system. 
 The outcomes are direct: faster reporting regardless of IT experience, significantly higher data quality and completeness, and accelerated resolution by eliminating the manual follow-up that typically accompanies incomplete notifications. 

 Operational Maintenance Order Planning Agent 
 Turn a notification into a fully structured maintenance order with reference, readiness checks, and scheduling in one flow. 
 Once a notification exists, the Operational Maintenance Order Planning Agent takes over the planning step. It creates maintenance orders directly from open notifications or from scratch, and it can retrieve a recommended list of reference orders ranked by match score against equipment, work center, description, and recent history, so planners reuse proven structures rather than starting blank. 
 The agent executes readiness checks across all order prerequisites: component availability, service lead times, production resources and tools (PRTs), and capacity constraints. It validates dates against lead times, buffers, and resource availability. Status management (ready, in execution, scheduling, locked, tack/untack) is handled. 
 After order creation, the agent naturally prompts the planner to bundle the order into an existing or new maintenance event, bridging directly into the event planning workflow described below. 

 Maintenance Event Planning Agent 
 Group, assign, and coordinate maintenance work across events without manual backlog triage. 
 The Maintenance Event Planning Agent addresses one of the more labor-intensive aspects of tactical planning: aligning work orders and notifications to the right maintenance event (for example, a planned shutdown). Planners currently spend significant time manually reviewing backlog and assigning items; this agent automates that identification and matching. 
 The agent creates maintenance events by event type (configurable per system), assigns relevant orders and notifications based on technical object and planning attributes, and provides visibility into assigned work and potential blockers within each event. It also identifies backlog items that fall within the event scope but have not yet been assigned, reducing the risk of leaving relevant work out of a window. 
 Planners can ask for open events by time range ("show me events from October 1 to October 10"), assign additional orders conversationally, and release the planning bucket, all within the same Joule session. 

 Maintenance Job Debrief Agent 
 Capture what actually happened in the field, even from a handwritten note or a photo. 
 The Maintenance Job Debrief Agent is built for the technician to complete a job. Its purpose is to make job confirmation and knowledge capture fast and natural, regardless of how the technician prefers to document work. A photo of the asset you just worked on, a handwritten note, an informal description: the agent reads all of it and converts it into structured, system-ready confirmation data. 
 The agent finds the relevant order and operational line items from the provided context, corrects spelling, structures work details, and guides the posting of time and material usage, both planned and unplanned. When multiple jobs need confirmation, the agent handles them in sequence within the same session. 
 Once confirmation is complete, the agent generates a structured feedback template, available in multiple languages, that the technician can review and send to the relevant planner. Crucially, the agent creates a draft in Outlook but does not send it automatically; the technician retains full control over what is communicated and to whom. This preserves operational knowledge at the point where it is richest: immediately after a job is completed. 

 Equipment Insights Agent 
 All equipment information in one view without manual data gathering across systems. 
 The Equipment Insights Agent brings together fragmented equipment information from across S/4HANA into a single, structured overview. It aggregates equipment master data, installation details, active orders and notifications, measurement documents, and historical maintenance records, and summarizes long texts automatically so users do not have to read a long source to understand an asset's recent history. 
 Beyond a static summary, the agent analyzes failure patterns, reliability indicators such as MTTR and MTBR (mean time to repair and mean time between repairs), and financial performance, linking cost data to maintenance and operational records. This gives maintenance planners, reliability engineers, and master data specialists a foundation for data-driven maintenance decisions and strategy. 
 The agent works on one equipment record at a time, presenting status, age, location, maintenance history, last service date, and next scheduled maintenance — a quick, comprehensive briefing on an asset, with recommendations on what to address next. 

 Maintenance Task List Agent 
 Build maintenance task lists from instruction manuals automatically and consistently. 
 The Maintenance Task List Agent automates the creation and maintenance of task lists by reading equipment instruction manuals (uploaded to customer-controlled storage such as SharePoint or S3). It extracts maintenance-relevant content based on the context provided by the planner, determines the appropriate operations and organizational attributes, and presents a draft task list for review and approval before any record is written. 
 The agent identifies whether an existing task list already exists for the equipment and reuses or updates it where applicable, rather than creating duplicates. It supports equipment task lists, functional location task lists, and general maintenance task lists. When a manual changes, the agent detects the differences and applies targeted updates, enabling consistent, scalable maintenance practices across growing asset fleets. 
 This capability requires document grounding functionality and a subscription to SAP BTP where the MCP server is deployed.

items.title: SAP Business One: 30 Years of Growing Together
items.author: Stefanie Glenk
items.text:
Turning 30 is a good reason to look back—and an even better moment to ask what comes next. For SAP Business One, SAP’s solution for small- and medium-sized customers, that means building on three decades of growth with small and mid-size businesses and adopting AI to open new possibilities for customers to prosper in the future. 

 Growing together 

 Customer satisfaction has long been a hallmark of SAP Business One, with an enviably high customer retention rate in the upper 90% range. Customers typically only leave the solution when a business ceases to exist, for example through bankruptcy or acquisition. “Looking back at the last 30 years, we’ve had almost no customer churn,” said Darius Heydarian, global head of Partner Enablement for SAP Business One. “Some customers started with a handful of employees and stayed through two or three decades of change, growing with the solution.” 

 Heydarian named two main reasons for the high customer retention: ongoing innovations in the solution itself and the SAP Business One partner ecosystem. SAP Business One operates on a fully indirect model: the solution is sold and implemented solely by partners, who also support customers during their day-to-day operations. Those partners are autonomous, locally present, and in many cases have been building solution expertise and knowledge for over 20 years. 

 Customer voices 

 Vereens Stores: adapting the software as operations evolve 

 Vereens Stores, a U.S.-based supplier of fertilizers and turf management solutions, has been with SAP Business One for over 20 years. Andee DiCola, chief financial officer and co-owner, points to one thing above all else as the reason for staying: the customization capabilities of SAP Business One. “Rather than having to change the way we operate to fit the software, we have been able to adapt SAP Business One to meet our needs,” she said. Looking ahead, she expects AI to help her company work smarter with information already available today. “I see opportunities around reporting, data analysis, identifying unusual transactions or exceptions, and helping automate repetitive processes.” 

 Design Resources, Inc.: using the same core platform across new ventures and markets 
 Experience a single, affordable ERP solution for managing your entire company with SAP Business One 

 Learn more 

 Design Resources, Inc. (DRI), which designs and sources branded apparel, runs multiple intradependent businesses on SAP Business One. Joe Leimer, chief information officer at DRI, said the solution’s flexibility has followed each new opportunity: “Whenever ownership is exploring a new venture, the flexibility of SAP Business One hasn’t been a limit for us. We know our core ERP needs will be handled and backed by SAP.” For Leimer, choosing an ERP platform “is a decision you only want to make once.” 

 Staying current: three decades of technology shifts 

 The roots of SAP Business One are in a business management solution built for small companies by an Israel-based startup called Top Manage, which was bought by SAP in 2002. 

 Renamed SAP Business One after the acquisition, the solution kept pace with—and sometimes led—technology shifts inside SAP. In 2011, it was one of the first SAP solutions to integrate the new SAP HANA in-memory database. That early adoption gave customers speed and analytics capabilities that traditional databases couldn’t match at the time. In 2020, SAP Business One, Web client, was introduced, encapsulating core business logic in a fresh and modernized user experience. Since then, the Web client has continued to evolve, delivering a growing scope of business processes alongside innovative analytics, integration, and customization capabilities. 

 SAP Business One version 11, open for initial partner preview in 2027, will introduce a new generation of cloud management tools for SAP partners, such as containerized lifecycle management, which allows software updates without system downtime. It also adds native deployment support for hyperscaler platforms including AWS, Microsoft Azure, and Google Cloud, as well as native cloud storage integration via Google Drive and OneDrive. 

 Adopting AI 

 In August 2026, SAP Business One introduced integrated generative AI capabilities: “Ask AI” and AI user-defined query. Ask AI allows users to select business data within SAP Business One, based on their individual user authorization, and ask contextual questions about it, such as researching shipping costs, delivery times, or alternatives for a product. AI user-defined query allows non-technical users to generate sharable lists using natural language; for example, “Show me the top five customers by outstanding payments.” 

 The partner AI ecosystem: two examples at work 

 Beyond native AI features within SAP Business One, a growing ecosystem of partner-built AI solutions is already live. MCP (Model Context Protocol) server integration offers partners new ways to build their own agents and AI-powered extensions for SAP Business One. SAP’s Global AI Partner Innovations Playbook lists 54 solutions to date, with many more to come. The following examples shine a light on the quality of solutions offered by the ecosystem. 

 Third Wave, a U.S.-based SAP partner, built Forge AI, an agentic AI that embeds seamlessly into SAP Business One, Web client. Users interact in natural language via a copilot window inside the SAP Business One user interface. They can search for a specific invoice, create a goods receipt, raise a support call, or cancel an order. The agent reads and writes data within SAP Business One, with a human confirmation step for any irreversible action. 

 SAP partner Cloudiax took a different approach. Best known as an SAP Business One hosting provider, Cloudiax built AXeLANT Chat, an agentic AI running entirely on its own NVIDIA infrastructure in Germany—purpose-built for companies with strict data privacy and sovereignty requirements. AXeLANT Chat both analyzes business data and, with a human in the loop, carries out tasks such as creating a sales quote in SAP Business One. 

 Built to last 

 Embedded AI will be the next big chapter of SAP Business One. “The upcoming version 11 of SAP Business One will be aligned with the Autonomous Enterprise strategy, enabling agentic AI capabilities for the Web client and further extensibility possibilities for partner AI innovation,” said Peter Dominik, global head of SAP Business One Product Management. 

 Joost Tigelaar, SAP global sales for SME Solutions, summarized the feedback from various conversations he had with partners during the SAP Partner Summit for EMEA and MEE in October: “SAP Business One customers value the flexibility of the solution, the strength of our partner ecosystem, and increasingly expect AI and automation to help them get more value from their business data and make every day work simpler.” 

 Thirty years after the first customers made the strategic decision to adopt SAP Business One, the solution continues to evolve alongside its customers and the 1.2 million users working with it every day.

items.title: Three Skills That Define the New Entry-Level Job in the AI Era
items.author: Lara Albert
items.text:
The first weeks—or even days—on a job look very different than they did a decade ago. What’s changing isn’t just the pace of work but how quickly you’re expected to contribute. 

 Early-career roles have long relied on gradual, hands-on learning: sitting in on meetings, preparing briefing materials, compiling inputs for reports, coordinating across teams, or shadowing customer conversations. These moments helped young professionals build judgment through repetition. Today, that model is evolving. Many of those tasks—reviewing customer feedback to identify trends, diagnosing why a campaign missed its targets, investigating a product bug or unexpected feature behavior, or interpreting performance metrics to suggest next steps—can now be completed in minutes with AI . Work that once filled weeks of onboarding is compressed into hours, fundamentally changing how learning happens on the job. 
 Early talent in peril: How HR can strategically select and develop the workforce of tomorrow 

 Read the research 

 As organizations adapt, the expectations placed on employees are evolving just as quickly. Recent SAP research found that nearly 69% of organizations say AI is expanding employees’ day-to-day responsibilities, while more than half say workforce upskilling and reskilling isn’t keeping pace with AI adoption. For early-career professionals, that means entering workplaces where execution is faster, responsibilities are broader, and human judgment is even more important. 

 Put together, the shift is clear. The new entry-level job brings higher expectations and less time to build confidence. In this environment, succeeding early in your career isn’t about knowing more—it’s about thinking differently. Three skills in particular will set you apart. 

 AI fluency isn’t enough—judgment is what sets you apart 

 Knowing how to use AI is quickly becoming table stakes. With 86% of students reporting they use AI in their studies, more than half weekly and nearly one in four daily, AI use alone won’t differentiate candidates. 

 What will differentiate them is judgment: how someone frames a problem, tests assumptions, and turns a draft into something others can actually use. 

 AI might give you a solid first draft of a client email, a slide deck, or a performance report. But is the tone right for that customer? Are the numbers interpreted correctly? Does the recommendation actually make sense in context? 

 Used well, AI doesn’t replace thinking; it accelerates it. Used poorly, it produces confident-sounding work that’s misaligned, unsupported, or simply wrong. 

 Before you hit send or share AI-assisted work, ask yourself: What problem am I solving? What might be missing or incorrect? What feels unclear or risky? And what should happen next? 

 This isn’t about overthinking everything. It’s about making sure your work holds up, not just that it gets done. 

 Make your work trustworthy 

 As AI speeds up production, trust becomes a constraint. Fast work only matters if people can trust it. And early in your career, trust is what determines how much responsibility you’re given. 

 Your role isn’t to accept AI output; it’s to validate it. 

 If you’re using AI to summarize a sales call, pull insights from a data set, or draft a response to a customer issue, your job is to check the details: Are the numbers accurate? Are the sources credible? Is anything missing? Does this align with how your company actually operates? 

 It also means knowing when to pause. If something doesn’t look right in a report or feels off in a customer message, asking a question is far more valuable than guessing. 

 Just as important is transparency. Saying, “I used AI to draft this, here’s what I verified, and here’s what I’m unsure about,” builds more credibility than presenting something as fully finished when it isn’t. 

 In practice, this shows up in small, but important ways: double-checking a metric before it goes into a dashboard, confirming details before sending a customer email, or validating assumptions before sharing a recommendation. 

 You’re not alone in feeling some skepticism about AI. Gallup’s Gen Z research shows adoption can be steady as confidence fluctuates, and that skepticism can be an advantage. When you channel it into stronger verification habits and higher standards of proof, you’re not just moving fast; you’re producing work others can trust. 

 Rapid learning is a competitive edge 

 The biggest advantage you have early in your career is how quickly you learn. 

 Every task—writing a follow-up email, building a slide, handling a support ticket, analyzing a report—is an opportunity to refine how you think. The professionals who progress fastest are the ones who treat each assignment as a learning loop, seeking input early, reflecting on outcomes, and applying lessons immediately. 

 That doesn’t require a complex system. It can be as simple as asking: What decision did I make? Why? What worked (or didn’t)? And what will I do differently next time? 

 This does two things: it converts experience into judgment faster, and it prevents AI from becoming a crutch. AI can generate options, but real growth comes from reviewing outcomes and adjusting how you work. 

 The entry-level job hasn’t disappeared, it’s evolved 

 Entry-level roles may be fewer and harder to secure, but the roles that exist today are shifting toward earlier responsibility as AI compresses execution time and pulls more meaningful work forward. 

 The core skills that matter most aren’t simply “using AI.” They are judgment, the ability to build trust in your work, and the discipline to keep learning. 

 If you get this right, you won’t just ramp quickly. You’ll stand out, building the kind of professional judgment, credibility, and confidence that no tool can replace.

items.title: I Passed the SAP Joule Studio Developer Exam. Here's What I Wish I'd Known.
items.author: shaktibarath
items.text:
I just passed the SAP Certified – Joule Studio Developer exam (C_JSD). If you work anywhere near SAP and AI agents, my advice is simple: take it now. 
 SAP is offering one free attempt at the exam until December 31, 2026. That alone is reason enough to stop circling it. But there is a better one. This is not a memorize-and-recall test. It asks you to build, reason and defend your choices, and the preparation teaches you how SAP actually thinks about agents in the enterprise. 
 Here is what worked, what didn't, and the one mistake I hope you avoid. 
 Before you start: claim your free attempt 

 Yes, it really is free. As part of the Joule Studio launch, SAP is giving every learner one attempt when they sign up through the campaign page on SAP Learning and accept the terms. You don't need an SAP Learning Hub subscription or a paid certification voucher. 
 There's a catch worth knowing: this free attempt is the only way to take the exam. SAP won't accept a paid attempt for it, so if your one try goes badly, there's no buying a second. Prepare accordingly. 
 Setup takes a few minutes. Do it in this order. 
 Check your SAP Universal ID. You need a valid one at account.sap.com . SAP recommends assigning two different email addresses to it. 
 Claim the complimentary attempt. Log in, accept the terms and claim your attempt . You get one free try, so don't rush into the exam. 
 Read the official details. Review the Joule Studio Developer page and SAP's FAQ so nothing surprises you on the day. 
 Start with the learning journey, and finish it 

 My preparation began and ended with SAP's learning journey, Developing with Joule Studio . Complete it end to end. Don't skim the modules you think you already know. 
 The journey does two jobs. It walks you through building agents in Joule Studio, step by step. It also lays out the vocabulary and the architecture the exam leans on. When the exam later asks you to explain a design decision, you will be drawing on that material, not on the clicks you made. 
 You'll find the journey on SAP Learning . By the end, you should be comfortable with four things: 
 Creating Joule agents 
 Extending existing agents 
 Building workflows 
 Explaining where Joule Studio fits within SAP Business AI 
 It's an assessment, not a quiz, so book early 

 The Joule Studio Developer exam is scenario-based, not multiple choice. You get two hours, and you need 60% to pass. The work is hands-on: you build agents in Joule Studio, complete practical exercises, then demonstrate what you built to an AI avatar. The avatar also zooms out to the big picture, so expect to discuss how your work fits into the wider enterprise. 
 SAP supplies a pre-configured Joule Studio practice environment, so you don't need your own BTP subaccount or Joule Studio subscription. The catch is the clock. Once you enroll in that environment, you have 24 hours to complete the hands-on exercises, build the required agents and finish the certification assessment. 
 That makes timing everything. Don't activate the practice system until your preparation is done. But don't leave it to the last week either. More people are taking the exam while it's free, and availability could tighten as the deadline nears. 
 Read the intent, requirements and specifications like a contract 

 If I could underline one piece of advice, it would be this. Read everything Joule Studio generates for an agent: the intent, the requirements and the specifications. Don't treat them as boilerplate you scroll past on the way to the build. 
 Those artifacts are where the agent's purpose gets pinned down. They define what it should do, what it shouldn't, and how success is judged. The exam returns to them repeatedly, and you will be asked to review them critically, not just accept them. Know where they come from, how they connect, and what a weak one looks like. 
 The mistake I made: don't deploy the agent 

 Here is where I lost time. During practice, I deployed my agent. It felt like the thorough, real-world thing to do. Instead, I ran straight into issues, including IAS errors/permissions, that had nothing to do with what the exam measures. 
 The exam runs your agent with mock data. Deployment isn't part of the task. Every minute I spent untangling permissions issues was a minute I didn't spend testing my agent's logic. 
 So learn from me: build the agent, test it with mock data, and stop there. Save deployment for your real projects. 
 Inside the exam: a conversation, not a form 

 The most memorable part was the format. The exam opens with an AI role-play agent. It asks you to open Joule Studio and walk it through a custom agent, in my case one built to review billing. 
 From there, it feels less like an exam and more like a design review with a sharp colleague. You look at the agent's initial prompt. You review its intent and requirements. You are expected to ask clarifying questions where something is vague, which is exactly what a good developer does with a fuzzy business request. Later, the conversation moved on to reviewing an extension in the financial close space, focused on escalations. 
 Once the build review is done, the agent zooms out to the big picture. The conversation shifts from the agent you built to how agents operate across the enterprise: how they're governed, how they connect to other systems, and where people stay in control. That's where your broader preparation pays off. 
 Study the big picture, not just the build 

 Building an agent gets you in the door. Understanding where it fits in the enterprise gets you through. Before the exam, spend time with SAP's wider story on Business AI, including the Autonomous Enterprise vision and the SAP AI Agent Hub. Read SAP's own material on them, not just summaries, so you understand the thinking behind the products as well as the features. 
 Don't stop at definitions. Ask yourself why SAP designed things the way it did, and what trade-offs those choices involve. 
 A feature list tells you what the platform does. The reasoning behind it tells you when to use it, and that's what you'll need to explain. 
 Then make it concrete. Pick a business process you know well, from your own projects or clients, and walk through it end to end. 
 Where would an agent genuinely help? 
 Where would you still want a person making the call? 
 What would you need to see to trust the agent once it's running? 
 You don't need perfect answers. You need to have thought it through before someone asks. 
 Finally, practice saying it out loud. Explaining a design choice in a conversation is a different skill from understanding it on paper. 
 If you can talk a colleague through your reasoning in a few clear sentences, you're ready. The exam rewards a clear point of view grounded in how the platform works, not memorized answers. 
 If you remember only five things 

 Claim your free attempt before December 31, 2026. 
 Complete the Developing with Joule Studio learning journey in full. 
 Read every generated intent, requirement and specification closely. 
 Start the 24-hour practice window only when you're ready, and test with mock data. Don't deploy. 
 Practice explaining your design choices, because the exam will ask you to. 
 Knowing what Joule is won't set you apart for long. Knowing how to build with it will. The credential is worth having, and the thinking it forces is worth even more. 
 I hope my experience helps you walk into the exam a little more prepared and a little less anxious, and walk out with a pass. 
 If you've taken it already, or you're preparing now, please share your experience in the comments. Your tips might be exactly what the next person needs. I read every comment and will reply as time permits. 
 Good luck. I'm rooting for you.

Joule evolves from a conversational interface into an agentic orchestration layer featuring open protocol support and expanded third-party connectivity. SAP Business AI Platform connects them to business context with governance at scale.

 * **Invoice posting:** BSET correctly separates both lines with their respective GL accounts and transaction keys (MWS and ZP1). 
 * **Transfer execution (RFUMSV50):** The program triggers warning message FF707 and forces the ZP1 transaction key onto the VAT line in the target document (F2), corrupting the VAT report (S_ALR_87012357). 
 **Pricing & Configuration Setup:** 
 * Tax procedure: TAXMX (Mexico). 
 * Source Deferred Tax Code: I2 (MWS for VAT, ZP1 for IEPS). 
 * Target Tax Code: F2. 
 * OBCN configuration: ZP1 is configured with Tax Class = blank or 3 (Additional tax), while MWS uses Tax Class 1. 
 **Our Questions:** 
 1. Has anyone encountered this limitation in DEFTAX when handling mixed tax codes (VAT + IEPS) in Mexico? 
 2. Since SAP standard does not cover this multi-line preservation of `KTOSL` in `RFUMSV50`, what is the cleanest way to implement an **Enhancement (Implicit/Explicit Enhancement)** to force the program to read the original `KTOSL` values directly from table `BSET` for the target documents without breaking standard execution? 
 Any advice, code pointers, or architecture recommendations would be greatly appreciated. Thank you!

Hi SAP Community, 
 I am looking for guidance on the correct line-item looping/context configuration in the SAP Integration Suite Managed Gateway Mapping Tool. 
 Requirement 
 For inbound cXML InvoiceDetailRequest, we need to map the service line description: 

 InvoiceDetailServiceItemReference/Description 
 to: 
 Plain Text 
 ARBCIG_INVOIC 
 /IDOC 
 /E1EDP01 
 /E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS 
 /JOBDESC 
 SAP's cXML invoice structure supports InvoiceDetailItem for regular invoice lines and InvoiceDetailServiceItem for service-specific lines. 
 Current behavior 
 The mapping works when there is only one service occurrence. 
 Examples tested successfully: 
 1 Material 
 2 Materials 
 2 Materials + 1 Service 
 The issue appears when there are multiple service occurrences: 

 Service + Service 
 2 Materials + 2 Services 
 For example: 
 Source Service 1: 
 Description = Service Description A 

 Source Service 2: 
 Description = Service Description B 
 Expected: 
 Service 1 → JOBDESC = Service Description A 
 Service 2 → JOBDESC = Service Description B 
 Actual: 
 Service 1 → JOBDESC = Service Description A 
 Service 2 → JOBDESC = Service Description A 

 The first service description is therefore reused for the subsequent service line. 
 Current source conditions 
 The mapping originally contained: 

 C1: 
 Type = VALUE 
 Operator = NOTEMPTY 
 XPath = InvoiceDetailServiceItem/@invoiceLineNumber 

 C2: 
 Type = POSITION 
 Operator = EQUALS 
 Position = 1 

 Source Expression: 
 C1 AND C2 
 This results in a generated XPath containing: 

 InvoiceDetailServiceItem[1] 
 With this configuration, the Mapping Tool Extension Transformation succeeds, but the first service description is reused for the second service item. 
 Diagnostic test 
 We removed only: 
 C2 = POSITION EQUALS 1 
 and retained: 

 C1 = invoiceLineNumber NOTEMPTY 
 The Mapping Tool Extension Transformation then failed with: 

 A sequence of more than one item is not allowed 
 as the first argument of fn:string-length() 
 The error contains both service descriptions: 

 ("Service Description A", "Service Description B") 
 This seems to indicate that, without the position restriction, the Description XPath returns multiple service-item values in the same evaluation context rather than one value per service occurrence. 
 Question 
 What is the recommended way to loop/map each: 

 InvoiceDetailServiceItem 
 /InvoiceDetailServiceItemReference 
 /Description 
 to the corresponding: 

 E1EDP01 
 /E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS 
 /JOBDESC 
 when more than one InvoiceDetailServiceItem exists? 
 Specifically: 
 Should this use a Target Position Variable against a repeating target structure? 
 Would a Target Value Variable using invoiceLineNumber or lineNumber be more appropriate? 
 If using a Target Value Variable, which ARBCIG_INVOIC target field should be used as the matching sequential value? 
 Has anyone implemented this mapping successfully for cXML invoices containing both InvoiceDetailItem and multiple InvoiceDetailServiceItem occurrences? 
 SAP documentation describes Target Position Variable looping by selecting the repeating target parent and applying the corresponding source condition. 
 SAP also documents Target Value Variable looping for cases where a source sequential value can be matched with the corresponding target sequential value. 
 Any working example for InvoiceDetailServiceItem → ARBCIG_INVOIC would be greatly appreciated. 
 Thank you.

Looking for exact steps to apply patch SAP19P_2608-70004550 for a system with RAC. 
 Need clarification if we have a rac system do we stop the instance on one node and focus only on that servers patching? 
 Is this patch a rolling patch and we can keep the instance running on the other server? We have a two node rac cluster with ASM being used. 
 Unless otherwise stated, non-rolling installation steps that need to be executed on more than one cluster node can be executed in parallel on all nodes of the cluster. However, you must wait for all parallel executions related to one installation step to complete before moving to the next installation step. 
 Follow the steps below. 

 Stop all database applications, in particular all SAP applications. 

 For each node of the cluster* and for each RDBMS home controlled by the grid stack* , stop all CRS-managed resources associated with the RDBMS home: rm -f $OHRDBMS.`hostname`.srvctlstatus env ORACLE_HOME=$OHRDBMS ORACLE_BASE=$OHRDBMS.dummybase $OHRDBMS/bin/srvctl stop home -o $OHRDBMS \ -s $OHRDBMS.`hostname`.srvctlstatus -n `hostname` 
 Above command and, likewise, other commands referring to the srvctl utility in this document intentionally use a dummy ORACLE_BASE directory to avoid errors when file orabasetab has not been maintained yet in some Oracle Home. See SAP Note 1521371 Setting of ORACLE_BASE in SAP environments for details. 

 After having shut down all database processes as described in the previous step, use the fuser OS command to check for stale SQL*Plus sessions for each node of the cluster* and for each RDBMS home controlled by the grid stack* : # temporarily change to super user su root -c "$SBPFUSER $IHRDBMS/bin/oracle" 
 If that command reports running processes, these are stale SQL*Plus sessions, which you can safely terminate with the kill command. 

 For systems using ACFS only* : 
 For each node of the cluster* , use the fuser OS command to check whether there are active processes running on any ACFS file system: # temporarily change to super user su root -c "/sbin/acfsutil info fs -o mountpoints | xargs $SBPFUSER -mu" 
 If that command reports running processes, shut them down cleanly to avoid their forced termination in the next step. 

 For each node of the cluster* , shut down the grid stack and unlock the grid home for patching: # temporarily change to super user su root -c "$OHGRID/crs/install/rootcrs.sh -prepatch -nonrolling" 

 For Linux x86-64 only: 
 For each node of the cluster* , take note of owner, group, and permissions of the oradism executable, then ensure that MOPatch can overwrite that executable: ls -al $OHGRID/bin/oradism # temporarily change to super user su root -c "chown `id -u` $OHGRID/bin/oradism && chmod u+rw $OHGRID/bin/oradism" 

 For each node of the cluster* , install the patches of the SAP Bundle Patch into the grid home: env ORACLE_HOME=$OHGRID $OHGRID/MOPatch/mopatch.sh -v -s SGR19P_2608-70004550.ZIP 
 Check the generated MOPatch reports for errors or unresolved conflicts. To resolve them, refer to section 6, "Known Issues" and to section "Resolving Patch Conflicts and Errors" of SAP Note 1027012 MOPatch - Install Multiple Oracle Patches in One Run. 
 Furthermore, check whether MOPatch has deinstalled any non-SBP patches and ensure that you have not lost any critical fixes because of this. 

 For Linux x86-64 only: 
 For each node of the cluster* , restore owner, group, and permissions of the oradism executable and verify that they are identical to those they had in the beginning: # temporarily change to super user su root -c "chown root $OHGRID/bin/oradism && chmod 4750 $OHGRID/bin/oradism" ls -al $OHGRID/bin/oradism

6.summary: A how-to for filtering a Fiori elements List Report on a RAP header by a field that lives on the item (child) entity. The author argues this is an OData V4 Fiori elements filter problem, so you should not join or denormalise item fields into the header. The approach is to expose the composition path in the selection annotation and let RAP and the UI layer handle it. The excerpt is only a bullet summary, so the full code, XML and annotation examples are not visible.
key_points: Filtering a header list by an item field is treated as an OData V4 / Fiori elements filter problem, not a reason to denormalise items into the header.
RAP supports any-depth compositions out of the box; the author recommends testing the filter in the browser first.
Add the navigation path (_Item/Field) to the UI.SelectionFields annotation.
A local UI.SelectionFields annotation replaces the backend one, so the full list of selection fields must be repeated in the local annotation.
If the FilterBar fails with "reading 'map'", the author attributes it to a problem in the XML (annotation) and says to check it.
The source has a typo in the bullet ("UI.SelectionFietions"); the intended annotation is UI.SelectionFields.
technical_details: UI.SelectionFields annotation with a navigation path such as _Item/Field
RAP business object with a header-to-item composition
OData V4 Fiori elements List Report and FilterBar
Local (metadata/UI) annotation overriding the backend annotation set
Error message in the FilterBar: reading 'map' (attributed to XML)
6.why_it_matters: Filtering a header list by child-item data is a very common requirement in Fiori apps. The useful point is the design choice: keep the BO model normalised and push the filter through the composition path, rather than duplicating data into the header. The override behaviour of local annotations is also a common source of missing filter fields.
6.teaching_angle: Build a header/item RAP BO with a composition, then add a UI.SelectionFields entry using the _Item/Field path. Have students deliberately create a local annotation that overrides the backend list and see which filter fields disappear. Discuss why denormalising item fields into the header is a poor design. Use the 'reading map' FilterBar error as a debugging exercise on annotation XML.

52.summary: A detailed question about mapping several cXML InvoiceDetailServiceItem descriptions to the same JOBDESC field in an ARBCIG_INVOIC IDoc segment using the SAP Integration Suite Managed Gateway Mapping Tool. A single service line maps correctly, but with two or more service lines every service gets the first description. The poster shows that a POSITION EQUALS 1 condition causes the XPath to contain InvoiceDetailServiceItem[1], and that removing it leads to a fn:string-length error where the argument is a sequence of both descriptions. They ask how to loop each service item to its own E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS segment and whether Target Position or Target Value Variable looping is appropriate. No answer is included.
key_points: Mapping works with one service line but reuses the first service description when there are two or more
The hard-coded POSITION EQUALS 1 condition makes the generated XPath InvoiceDetailServiceItem[1]
Removing the position condition makes the Description XPath return a sequence, causing a fn:string-length error
The diagnostic error shows both descriptions returned in one evaluation context, which suggests the source is not scoped per occurrence
The poster asks whether Target Position Variable or Target Value Variable looping, using invoiceLineNumber or lineNumber, should be used
No solved example is included in the post
technical_details: SAP Integration Suite Managed Gateway Mapping Tool, cXML InvoiceDetailRequest inbound
Target: IDOC /E1EDP01 /E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS /JOBDESC, ARBCIG_INVOIC
Source: InvoiceDetailServiceItem/InvoiceDetailServiceItemReference/Description
Conditions: C1 VALUE NOTEMPTY on InvoiceDetailServiceItem/@invoiceLineNumber, C2 POSITION EQUALS 1, expression C1 AND C2
Generated XPath InvoiceDetailServiceItem[1]
Error: A sequence of more than one item is not allowed as the first argument of fn:string-length()
52.why_it_matters: Looping in the CIG mapping tool is a common blocker for cXML invoice projects with repeating line items. The post gives a precise, reproducible diagnostic that is more useful than most mapping questions.
52.developer_problem: How to make each repeated InvoiceDetailServiceItem description map to its own E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS/JOBDESC segment in the CIG mapping tool when there are several service items, instead of reusing the first one.
52.teaching_angle: A strong case study for teaching source and target context in graphical mapping tools. Ask students to predict the generated XPath for each condition set before running the test, then discuss why a fixed position index works for one line but not for a repeating set. Compare Target Position and Target Value looping and explain why a sequential key such as invoiceLineNumber must exist on the target side.

The unit value was read from characteristic ATWRT in AUSP via batch objects from INOB
A bad characteristic value was found in the batch classification

Root cause not identified; title refers to a different issue (unit BOT, language EN)

49.developer_problem: How to stop RFUMSV50 from replacing the VAT line's transaction key with the IEPS key for mixed deferred tax codes, and where to add an enhancement that keeps the original KTOSL values from BSET.

Students should first find out which enhancement points exist in RFUMSV50 (for example with the enhancement tools in SE80), then check whether a standard note or support package changes the behaviour before writing custom code. digest.headline: A thin ABAP day: one RAP filter how-to, plus unanswered questions on Joule, MCP, UI Adaptation and API gaps.
digest.overview:
The only core-stack item today is a RAP how-to on filtering a Fiori elements List Report by a field on a child item. The advice is to add the composition path (_Item/Field) to UI.SelectionFields and not to denormalise item data into the header. A local UI.SelectionFields annotation replaces the backend one, so the full list must be repeated there. The excerpt is a bullet summary, so the code is not visible.

The rest is mostly unanswered community questions and teaser posts. Joule and custom Z-tables, MCP with ECC, and the Special G/L gap in the clearing API all concern how much a released interface exposes. The UI Adaptation label question and the CIG mapping loop problem are troubleshooting cases. Several posts (refs 8, 14, 36, 73) show only an introduction, so treat their technical claims as unverified.

top_stories.title: Filtering a RAP List Report by a child-item field
top_stories.summary: The author treats this as an OData V4 Fiori elements filter problem. Add the navigation path (_Item/Field) to UI.SelectionFields. A FilterBar error "reading 'map'" is attributed to a problem in the annotation XML.

deep_dives.title: Filtering a RAP List Report by a child-item field
deep_dives.explanation:
The case is a header List Report that must be filtered by a field on an item entity in the composition. The source recommends against copying the item field into the header. Instead, expose the navigation path through the selection-field annotation, so the OData V4 Fiori elements filter bar applies the filter over the composition. It then relies on RAP's composition support and the OData V4 service.

The annotation entry is a path such as `_Item/Field` in `UI.SelectionFields`. In a CDS metadata extension the shape is roughly `@UI.selectionField: [{position: 10}]` on elements. For path-based fields, the source describes adding the navigation path to `UI.SelectionFields`. I cannot confirm the exact syntax from the excerpt, so verify it in your own system.

A local `UI.SelectionFields` annotation, for example in the app's annotation file, replaces the backend one. So if you add one path locally, you must repeat all existing selection fields, or they vanish from the filter bar. If the FilterBar fails with "reading 'map'", the author attributes it to a problem in the annotation XML, so inspect it first.

The design point is that the BO stays normalised. Denormalising item fields into the header duplicates data and needs synchronisation logic in the behaviour implementation.

deep_dives.title: Looping repeated items in the CIG mapping tool
deep_dives.explanation:
The poster maps cXML InvoiceDetailServiceItem descriptions to JOBDESC in the E1ARBCIG_NONPOSERV_DETAILS segment of ARBCIG_INVOIC. With one service line it works. With two or more, every target gets the first description.

The cause shown in the post is the condition C2, POSITION EQUALS 1, combined with C1 (invoiceLineNumber not empty). It generates an XPath with `InvoiceDetailServiceItem[1]`, so the first item is always selected. Removing C2 makes the Description XPath return a sequence of both descriptions. That sequence is then passed to `fn:string-length`, which accepts only a single item, hence the error.

This indicates the source is not scoped to the current occurrence. The poster asks whether Target Position or Target Value Variable looping, keyed on invoiceLineNumber or lineNumber, is the right approach. No answer is given, so treat it as an open diagnostic. The general principle is that a repeating target segment needs a loop context from the source, not a fixed index.
key_concepts: Source and target context in mapping
Sequence vs single item in XPath functions
Target Position vs Target Value Variable looping

interview_questions.question: A RAP List Report on a header needs a filter on an item field. How would you do it, and what pitfalls exist?
interview_questions.answer: Keep the model normalised and do not copy the item field into the header. Expose the composition navigation path, such as _Item/Field, in the UI.SelectionFields annotation so the OData V4 Fiori elements filter bar can filter through the composition. Test it in the browser first. The main pitfall is that a local UI.SelectionFields annotation replaces the backend one, so the complete list of selection fields must be repeated, or the existing ones disappear. If the FilterBar fails with a "reading 'map'" error, the annotation XML is the first thing to inspect. Denormalising would duplicate data and force you to keep it consistent in the behaviour implementation.

interview_questions.question: A UI Adaptation label change was transported but is not visible at runtime. How do you troubleshoot?
interview_questions.answer: Start by confirming the adaptation was made for the exact app ID and layer that is being run. Then confirm the transport was imported into the target system and client. Clear the browser and launchpad cache and retest with the same user and role. Check whether the label comes from an annotation or DDIC text that takes precedence over the adaptation. Finally, check whether each app uses its own label for the same field, since KNVV-KVGR2 appears in two apps. The source post gives no details, so each of these is a hypothesis to test, not a confirmed cause.

interview_questions.question: How would you design access for an LLM agent calling a legacy ECC system through an MCP server?
interview_questions.answer: The key decision is the identity the call runs under. A shared technical user is simple but breaks authorisation checks and audit trails, because every action looks like the same user. Per-user authentication preserves the business user's authorisations, but needs a mechanism to propagate identity through the MCP server and Integration Suite to ECC. First establish the ECC release, the connectivity method and the exact endpoints to expose. Expose only narrow, governed interfaces, not raw tables. The source post only raises the question and gives no solution, so any design must be validated against current documentation.
